entries.title: How municipalities organise policy implementation under weak enforcement
entries.abstract: Municipalities in Spain are subject to legal transparency requirements that are weakly enforced. This article examines how municipalities organise implementation under weak enforcement: how arrangements change over time, who takes responsibility and what prompts them to change. Drawing on 51 interviews with officers in charge of transparency in municipalities of varying sizes and compliance levels, we trace how implementation has evolved since 2010. We find that municipalities typically assign transparency duties to existing staff and structures, rather than creating dedicated roles. Although legal enactment often initiates implementation, moves towards more specialised arrangements are associated with external incentives, such as evaluations or rankings, rather than with legal enactment alone. entries.title: Corruption Perceptions, the Pendleton Act, and Sovereign Borrowing Costs
entries.abstract: ABSTRACT Significant research suggests that systems of bureaucratic patronage tend to promote corruption and reduce the efficient production of publicly provided goods. However, much less work has been done to consider how market actors perceive such selection processes and especially reforms implemented to reduce such corruption. This study rectifies this by evaluating how the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act impacted federal borrowing costs. If patronage resulted in increased corruption and bureaucratic inefficiency, this should be reflected in relatively higher bond yields. entries.title: Interpersonal trust in the policy advisory process: a research agenda
entries.abstract: Interpersonal trust is a key factor determining whether advice is taken into account in policy making, yet it has received little substantive attention in scholarship on policy advice and expert knowledge. Its role has only grown in importance amid accelerating democratic backsliding and the increased personalisation of politics in many jurisdictions. This article argues that policy scholarship can build on insights from other social science disciplines, which have a long-standing and rich tradition of researching trust, to develop a more purposeful and systematic approach to analysing interpersonal trust and its role in policy making. It sets out a research agenda for studying the phenomena that advances understanding of the informal dimensions of policy making, which have largely remained elusive. entries.title: “Unseen and unheard”: Recognition and Its Role in Shaping Administrative Burden
entries.abstract: Abstract Administrative burden scholarship has identified psychological costs alongside learning and compliance costs, yet the category remains homogeneous, grouping stigma, diminished autonomy, and stress, without a shared organizing principle. This article advances a mechanism-level account centered on recognition, drawing on a qualitative case study of claiming disability benefits in Israel, based on in-depth interviews with 33 individuals (16 young adults with diagnosed mental health conditions and 17 social and outreach workers). We argue that recognition, and its denial, are part of the mechanism through which psychological costs are produced, and that whether an encounter carries a message about a person's standing sorts the category into three analytically distinct types.
